content: 1. Multivariable-adjusted Cox regression analysis was employed to investigate the relationship between strength-promoting exercise (SPE) and mortality. This included examining any SPE, low-/high-volume SPE, and adherence to SPE guidelines (defined as ≥2 sessions per week). 2. The core study sample consisted of 80,306 adults aged 30 years or older, with a total of 5,763 deaths from any cause recorded over 736,463 person-years of follow-up. 3. The findings support the promotion of adherence to strength exercise guidelines as a priority, beyond generic physical activity targets. 4. Physical activity was assessed using a questionnaire that inquired about participation in sports and exercises during the four weeks preceding the interview. Participants were shown a card listing 10 exercise groupings, including gym-based activities (e.g., weight training, exercise biking) and own-body-weight exercises (e.g., push-ups, sit-ups). 5. The outcomes analyzed included all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, and cancer mortality. 6. A meta-analysis by Stanmore et al. (2017) evaluated the effects of active video games (exergames) on cognitive functioning in clinical and non-clinical populations. The study included 17 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with data from 926 participants. 7. Exergames were found to improve executive functions, attentional processing, and visuospatial skills. These findings represent the first meta-analytic evidence of exergames' effects on cognition. 8. Future research should identify patient and treatment factors influencing the efficacy of exergames and explore the neurobiological mechanisms underlying their effects. 9. A systematic review by Stutz et al. (2019) investigated the impact of evening exercise on sleep. The analysis included 23 studies and found no evidence to support the hypothesis that evening exercise negatively affects sleep. In fact, the opposite was observed. 10. However, vigorous exercise ending within one hour of bedtime may impair sleep-onset latency, total sleep time, and sleep efficiency. 11. A meta-analysis by Sultana et al. (2019) examined the effects of low-volume high-intensity interval training (HIIT) on body composition and cardiorespiratory fitness in normal weight, overweight, and obese adults. The analysis included 47 studies. 12. Low-volume HIIT was found to be ineffective for reducing total body fat mass or percentage compared to non-exercise controls and moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT). However, it significantly improved cardiorespiratory fitness, making it a time-efficient strategy for increasing fitness levels. 13. A systematic review by Shan et al. (2017) assessed the effects of Tai Chi on quality of life in perimenopausal women. Five trials were included, showing significant improvements in bodily pain, general health, vitality, and mental health, as well as spine bone mineral density. 14. Tai Chi may be recommended as an effective and safe adjunct treatment for perimenopausal syndrome, though more high-quality RCTs are needed to confirm these findings. 15. Across these studies, the methodologies included systematic reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs, with outcomes addressing various health domains such as cognitive functioning, sleep quality, body composition, cardiorespiratory fitness, and quality of life.
